Executive Summary

5/10

Stable bow arm and stance; the aim phase is where the shot breaks down.

  • Strongest: bow-arm extension held at 173.5° S1
  • Weakest: draw-elbow instability during aim, 76.6° with a 152.4° range W1
  • Injury watch: repetitive high-load flexion at the draw elbow
  • Consistency: not assessable from one shot
Full analysis
Estimated technical levelThe athlete demonstrates a stable stance and bow-arm extension but suffers from severe draw-elbow collapse during the aim phase, resulting in a critically low angle of 76.6 deg with high variability.
Overall technique score5/10 (from Section 12)
Strongest technical characteristicBow-arm stability is maintained throughout the shot cycle, with the elbow angle held near extension at 173.5 deg and minimal deviation. S1
Most important weaknessSevere instability and excessive flexion of the draw elbow during the AIM phase, dropping from 128.6 deg to 76.6 deg with a massive range of 152.4 deg. W1
Main consistency limitationShot-to-shot consistency is NOT RELIABLY ASSESSABLE FROM AVAILABLE VIDEO because only one shot was analysed, limiting the assessment to within-shot biomechanics.
Main biomechanical limitationThe draw arm fails to maintain structural integrity during aiming, indicated by the drop in elbow angle to 76.6 deg and excessive vertical center of gravity sway of 0.071 SW.
Main injury-risk factorRepetitive high-load flexion at the draw elbow joint during the aim phase may lead to tendon strain or instability in the anchor point due to the significant range of motion observed.
Most important correctionFocus on initiating the draw with scapular retraction to maintain a higher, more stable elbow position closer to 128.6 deg and reduce reliance on arm flexors. W1
Expected improvement opportunityStabilizing the draw elbow angle during the aim phase will secure the anchor point, reduce vertical sway, and improve arrow flight consistency by ensuring efficient force transfer.

Frame-by-Frame Shot Analysis

9 steps

We split the shot into 9 steps. We can trust 5 of them well and the other 4 fairly well.

  • Most of the time went on three steps: getting set (67 seconds), getting ready to draw (39 seconds) and aiming (27 seconds)
  • Draw and Anchor went by too fast to measure well, under 0.2 seconds each. The Draw time is probably a measuring mistake, not how long the draw really took
  • The bow arm stayed almost straight the whole time (about 165° to 179°, where 180° is fully straight)

Angle measurement space

Every joint angle is measured twice. The image plane value is what the joint subtends in the frame, in pixels, and is the value drawn on the annotated video and quoted throughout this report: it is the only one a reader can check against the picture. The world value is the same angle in the pose model's 3D landmarks, whose depth is inferred from a single camera. Where the two disagree the joint is not square to the camera, the projected angle is foreshortened, and its confidence is dropped to LOW.

Top Strengths

5 established

Five strengths, all HIGH confidence. Protect these while fixing the rest.

  • S1 Stable bow-arm extension during aiming
  • S2 Minimal lateral shoulder tilt
  • S3 Upright trunk posture in stance
  • S4 Low shoulder-hip separation in pre-draw
  • S5 Stable bow-arm follow-through
Full analysis
1. Stable bow-arm extension during aiming. S1 HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: Bow elbow angle is 173.5 deg with a small range of 6.7 deg. INTERPRETED: The minimal deviation indicates consistent skeletal support and reduced muscular fatigue in the bow arm during the aim phase.
Biomechanical reason: Maintaining a near-extended elbow angle minimizes the moment arm for gravity, reducing the load on the deltoid and triceps while providing a stable platform for the arrow rest.
Performance benefit: Consistent bow-arm stability reduces vertical sight pin oscillation, improving aim precision and shot-to-shot consistency.
Maintenance strategy: Continue reinforcing skeletal alignment cues to maintain this extension without hyperextension.
2. Minimal lateral shoulder tilt. S2 HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: Bow shoulder inclination is 94.6 deg with a range of 3.5 deg. INTERPRETED: The stability in the frontal plane suggests effective scapular stabilization and balanced muscle activation.
Biomechanical reason: A level shoulder girdle ensures that the draw force is transmitted directly along the arrow's line of travel, preventing torque-induced yaw errors.
Performance benefit: Prevents lateral arrow deflection upon release, enhancing accuracy.
Maintenance strategy: Monitor for asymmetry during fatigue; reinforce scapular retraction drills.
3. Upright trunk posture in stance. S3 HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: Trunk inclination is 0.5 deg. INTERPRETED: The near-vertical alignment keeps the center of gravity over the base of support, facilitating balance.
Biomechanical reason: An upright posture reduces shear forces on the lumbar spine and allows for efficient weight transfer through the legs during the draw.
Performance benefit: Provides a stable, balanced foundation that minimizes sway and improves consistency.
Maintenance strategy: Maintain core engagement to preserve this vertical alignment throughout the shot cycle.
4. Low shoulder-hip separation in pre-draw. S4 HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: Shoulder-hip separation is 2.7 deg. INTERPRETED: Minimal torsion between the upper and lower body indicates good alignment and readiness for a linear draw.
Biomechanical reason: Reducing pre-torque allows the athlete to generate power through sequential muscle activation rather than relying on elastic recoil from twisted tissues.
Performance benefit: Promotes a smoother, more controlled draw path and reduces energy leaks.
Maintenance strategy: Focus on foot placement and hip alignment to maintain this low separation.
5. Stable bow-arm follow-through. S5 HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: Bow elbow angle remains at 173.7 deg with a range of 0.9 deg. INTERPRETED: The lack of collapse or deviation after release indicates strong isometric control.
Biomechanical reason: Maintaining bow-arm position post-release prevents the bow from tipping, which could otherwise disturb the arrow's flight path during the critical initial milliseconds.
Performance benefit: Ensures consistent arrow clearance and reduces group dispersion.
Maintenance strategy: Practice holding the aim position for 2-3 seconds after release to reinforce stability.

Only 5 strengths could be reliably established from the available video.

1. Severe draw elbow instability and excessive flexion during AIM. W1 MEDIUM Priority HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: The draw elbow angle averages 76.6 deg with a massive range of 152.4 deg, indicating significant loss of structural integrity. INTERPRETED: This collapse suggests over-reliance on arm flexors rather than back extensors, leading to energy leakage.
Likely cause: Inadequate scapular retraction initiation and poor muscular endurance in the posterior chain during the aim phase.
Performance consequence: Destabilizes the anchor point and causes inconsistent arrow flight due to variable release timing and force application.
Correction: Focus on initiating the draw with scapular retraction to maintain a higher, more stable elbow position closer to 128.6 deg.
2. Excessive vertical center of gravity sway during AIM. W2 MEDIUM Priority HIGH
Evidence: MEASURED: The vertical COM sway range is 0.071 SW, which is substantial relative to the athlete's height. INTERPRETED: This vertical oscillation suggests instability in the knee and ankle joints, disrupting the stable platform required for aiming.
Likely cause: Poor balance control or excessive tension in the lower body leading to micro-adjustments.
Performance consequence: Causes the bow to move vertically relative to the target, resulting in vertical grouping errors.
Correction: Strengthen core stability exercises and focus on even weight distribution across the feet during the AIM phase.
3. Inconsistent anchor point distance from the face. W3 MEDIUM Priority MEDIUM
Evidence: MEASURED: The anchor distance range is 0.564 SW, indicating significant variation in hand position relative to the face. INTERPRETED: This inconsistency suggests a lack of tactile stability or scapular control during the draw-to-anchor transition.
Likely cause: Variable scapular retraction depth or inconsistent head position at anchor.
Performance consequence: Requires compensatory movements that strain the rotator cuff and lead to inconsistent sight pin alignment.
Correction: Improve scapular retraction stability during the draw phase. Use tactile cues to ensure consistent hand placement at the anchor point.
4. Neck inclination and head tilt variability. W4 HIGH Priority MEDIUM
Evidence: MEASURED: The neck inclination averages 14.1 deg with a range of 11.8 deg, and head tilt varies by 9.7 deg. INTERPRETED: This variability indicates poor head stability relative to the bow arm, affecting sight picture consistency.
Likely cause: Weakness in cervical stabilizers or tension in the trapezius muscles pulling the head out of alignment.
Performance consequence: Inconsistent sight pin placement and potential neck strain over repeated shots.
Correction: Focus on keeping the head neutral and stable relative to the anchor point. Strengthen neck stabilizers isometrically.
5. Draw elbow collapse during expansion. W5 LOW Priority MEDIUM
Evidence: MEASURED: The draw elbow angle drops to 27.4 deg during the expansion phase. INTERPRETED: This extreme flexion indicates a failure to maintain back tension and a reliance on arm strength to hold the draw, leading to instability.
Likely cause: Insufficient back muscle engagement or premature relaxation of the scapular retractors.
Performance consequence: Causes the bow to torque during release and reduces the effective draw weight felt at full draw.
Correction: Practice expansion drills focusing on keeping the draw elbow high and stable while extending the bow arm.

The athlete has a stable bow arm and good initial alignment but suffers from critical draw-arm instability and vertical sway during the aim phase. Focusing on scapular-driven drawing and lower-body stability will yield the most significant performance improvements.
